extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and practitioners preparing petitions to revive abandoned U.S. (and PCT-designating-U.S.) patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing and filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137 (including PTO/SB/64, PTO/SB/64a, PTO/SB/64/PCT forms) to revive an abandoned U.S. patent application (or PCT designating the U.S.) by establishing that the delay was unintentional and providing required items/fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement that the entire delay was unintentional
rubrics_metrics.description: "The entire delay in filing the required reply from the due date for the required reply until the filing of a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) was unintentional."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are advised to include the statement that the entire delay was unintentional, even if the applicant chooses to include a statement of facts concerning the delay. The USPTO may require additional information if there is a question whether the abandonment or the delay was unintentional (see MPEP 711.03(c) subsections (III)(C) and (D)). Applicants may use the Office forms (PTO/SB/64, PTO/SB/64a, or PTO/SB/64PCT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate course of action is not unintentional
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action on the part of the applicant does not become "unintentional" within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.137(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of deliberate reasons that will not be considered unintentional include: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over references in an outstanding Office action; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims of sufficient breadth to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to justify expense; (D) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to maintain interest; (E) applicant seeks to defer patent fees and prosecution expenses though remains interested in eventual patent. Case law (In re Application of G; In re Maldague) supports that a deliberate choice remains intentional even if the applicant later changes their mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in circumstances after abandonment does not render prior deliberate decision unintentional
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in circumstances that occurred subsequent to the abandonment of an application does not render 'unintentional' the delay resulting from a previous deliberate decision to permit an application to be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such post-abandonment changes only relate to why the deliberate decision was made, and do not convert an intentional abandonment into unintentional delay for petition purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Items required for a grantable petition (general PTO/SB/64)
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: A grantable petition requires the following items: (1) Petition fee; (2) Reply and/or issue fee; (3) Terminal disclaimer with disclaimer fee - required for all utility and plant applications filed before June 8, 1995; and for all design applications; and (4) Statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form PTO/SB/64 enumerates these required items; fees vary for small entity vs other than small entity (see 37 CFR 1.17(m) and claim small entity under 37 CFR 1.27). The reply may have been filed previously or be enclosed with the petition; issue/publication fees likewise may be previously paid or enclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Items required for revival when abandonment is for failure to notify of foreign/international filing (PTO/SB/64a)
rubrics_metrics.description: For petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(f) (failure to notify the Office of a foreign or international filing): petition fee; Notice of Foreign or International Filing (including filing date of subsequently filed foreign/international application); and statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form PTO/SB/64a requires the filing date of the subsequently filed foreign/international application. The USPTO may request additional information if the unintentional nature of the abandonment or the delay is in question. Fee treatment (small entity vs other) applies as in general petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Items required for revival of international (PCT) applications designating the U.S. (PTO/SB/64/PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: A grantable petition requires: (1) Petition fee; (2) Proper reply (the missing 35 U.S.C. 371(c) requirement(s)); (3) Terminal disclaimer with fee where required for international applications having an international filing date before June 8, 1995; and (4) Statement that the entire delay was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper reply consists of the missing 35 U.S.C. 371(c) items; the form PTO/SB/64/PCT asks whether such items have been filed previously or are enclosed. Terminal disclaimer rules and small-entity fee differences apply as noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirement and fee when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer (and disclaimer fee (37 CFR 1.20(d))) is required in certain circumstances: for utility/plant applications filed before June 8, 1995 and for all design applications (PTO/SB/64); for international applications with international filing date before June 8, 1995 (PTO/SB/64/PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms provide checkboxes/fields to enclose terminal disclaimer and indicate applicable fee (separate small entity vs other fees). If the application was filed on or after June 8, 1995, a terminal disclaimer may not be required (per form notes). See PTO/SB/63 for related terminal disclaimer guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of mailing or transmission requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing the petition, include a Certificate of Mailing or Transmission [37 CFR 1.8(a)] certifying deposit with the U.S. Postal Service as first-class mail with sufficient postage addressed to Mail Stop Petition, Commissioner for Patents, or transmission by facsimile to the USPTO, with date, signature, and typed/printed name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The forms include a Certificate of Mailing or Transmission block to record date, signature, and typed/printed name. This documents the method and date of sending the petition to the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid submitting unnecessary personal information
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner/applicant is cautioned to avoid submitting personal information in documents filed in a patent application that may contribute to identity theft, such as social security numbers, bank account numbers, or credit card numbers (other than payment forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such personal information is never required by the USPTO to support a petition or an application (except payment instruments). If included, applicants should consider redacting before submission. Applicants are advised that application records become public after publication or patent issuance; checks and credit card authorization forms PTO-2038 submitted for payment are not retained in the application file and are not publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small entity fee claim and fee amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition fee (and terminal disclaimer fee when applicable) have small entity and other-than-small-entity amounts; the form provides fields to indicate small entity claim (37 CFR 1.17(m); see 37 CFR 1.27).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants claiming small entity status should indicate it on the form; fee amounts differ depending on entity status. Failure to pay correct fee may affect grantability.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO may request additional information when unintentionality is in question
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States Patent and Trademark Office may require additional information if there is a question as to whether either the abandonment or the delay in filing a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) was unintentional (MPEP 711.03(c), subsections (III)(C) and (D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including a simple statement that the entire delay was unintentional accelerates treatment, but applicants should be prepared to submit supporting factual statements or evidence if the Office questions the claim of unintentional delay.
